items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a company that operates in more than one country, usually with headquarters in its home country”.
items.answer: Transnational corporation (TNC)
items.markingKey: Transnational corporation (TNC): a company that operates in more than one country, usually with headquarters in its home country. [1]

items.stem: Explain the new international division of labour.
items.answer: TNCs separate stages of production: high-skilled HQ, design and R&D in HICs; component making in NICs; assembly in low-wage countries; enabled by cheap transport and ICT.

items.stem: Explain why TNCs have become more powerful.
items.answer: Huge revenues, global supply chains and control of technology and brands; ability to move investment between countries gives bargaining power over governments; lobbying and tax planning.

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $44, Mexico $5, China $7, Vietnam $4, Bangladesh $2. Assembling a laptop takes 1.5 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 500 000 units a year. Calculate the annual saving in labour costs from assembling in the cheapest country rather than the USA.
items.answer: US$31 500 000 (Bangladesh)
items.markingKey: (US cost − cheapest cost) × 500 000 [2]

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $36, Mexico $4, China $10, Vietnam $3, Bangladesh $1.5. (b) Calculate the annual saving in labour costs from assembling in the cheapest country rather than the USA.
items.answer: (a) the USA: $43.2; Mexico: $4.8; China: $12; Vietnam: $3.6; Bangladesh: $1.8 (b) US$82 800 000 (Bangladesh)

items.stem: “TNCs are now more powerful than national governments.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to tax and revenue.
items.answer: For: Largest TNC revenues exceed many countries’ GDPs; footloose investment gives bargaining power; tax avoidance; lobbying. Against: Governments control regulation, taxation, trade policy and market access (China’s controls, EU fines on tech firms, global minimum tax agreement 2021); TNCs depend on states for infrastructure and stability. Conclusion: TNCs have great influence, especially over small countries, but large states retain significant power.

items.stem: Explain the reasons for the growth of TNCs.
items.answer: Falling transport and communication costs; trade liberalisation; access to markets and cheap labour and resources; economies of scale; mergers and acquisitions; government incentives.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the interconnected network of firms, suppliers and workers across several countries involved in making and selling a product”.
items.answer: Global production network
items.markingKey: Global production network: the interconnected network of firms, suppliers and workers across several countries involved in making and selling a product. [1]

items.stem: Explain why services are increasingly outsourced to countries such as India and the Philippines.
items.answer: Lower wages; large English-speaking, educated workforces; time-zone differences allowing 24-hour service; fast internet; government support for IT parks.

items.stem: Explain how global production networks distribute value between countries.
items.answer: High-value activities (R&D, design, branding, marketing) are in HICs and capture most value; low-value assembly in LICs captures little; upgrading allows countries to capture more.

items.stem: Fig. 27.2 shows the share of the retail price (US$1000) of a smartphone captured at each stage of its global production network: brand owner (design, software, marketing) 32%, component makers (chips, screen, memory) 34%, retail and distribution 10%, final assembly 2%, other costs 22%. (a) Calculate how many times more value the brand owner captures than final assembly. (b) Suggest why the brand owner keeps design and marketing in its home country.
items.answer: (a) 16 times (b) Highly skilled staff, universities and research clusters; protection of intellectual property; close to main markets and headquarters.

items.stem: Fig. 27.2 shows the share of the retail price (US$1000) of a smartphone captured at each stage of its global production network: brand owner (design, software, marketing) 35%, component makers (chips, screen, memory) 30%, retail and distribution 10%, final assembly 2%, other costs 23%. (a) Calculate the value captured at each stage. (b) Suggest why the brand owner keeps design and marketing in its home country.
items.answer: (a) brand owner (design, software, marketing): US$350; component makers (chips, screen, memory): US$300; retail and distribution: US$100; final assembly: US$20; other costs: US$230 (b) Highly skilled staff, universities and research clusters; protection of intellectual property; close to main markets and headquarters.

items.stem: “LICs gain little from participating in global production networks.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to value capture and working conditions.
items.answer: For: They capture a small share of value through low-wage assembly; footloose investment; poor working conditions (Rana Plaza 2013). Against: Jobs, export earnings, skills and technology transfer; upgrading (South Korea, Taiwan, China moved into higher value activities); India’s IT services sector. Conclusion: Gains are initially small, but countries that invest in skills and upgrading can capture more value over time.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a country that receives investment and operations from a foreign TNC”.

items.stem: Explain the advantages of TNC investment for host countries.
items.answer: Jobs and higher wages than local firms; skills and technology transfer; infrastructure; export earnings and tax revenue; multiplier effects through local suppliers.

items.stem: Explain the disadvantages of TNC investment for host countries.
items.answer: Low wages and poor conditions; profits repatriated; few local linkages; environmental damage; footloose plants may leave; competition harms local firms; political influence.

items.stem: A TNC invested US$1000 million in an electronics factory in Mexico. It employs 3 000 local workers at an average of US$2 400 a year. 51% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$156 million, of which 86% is repatriated to the home country. (a) Calculate the annual wage bill paid to local workers. (b) Calculate the investment per job created.
items.answer: (a) US$7.2 million (b) US$333 333

items.stem: A TNC invested US$200 million in an electronics factory in Mexico. It employs 1 500 local workers at an average of US$2 400 a year. 40% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$37 million, of which 67% is repatriated to the home country. (a) Calculate the profit repatriated and the profit retained in the host country each year. (b) Calculate the investment per job created.
items.answer: (a) repatriated US$24.8 million; retained US$12.2 million (b) US$133 333

items.stem: A TNC invested US$200 million in an electronics factory in India. It employs 1 500 local workers at an average of US$9 000 a year. 54% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$35 million, of which 62% is repatriated to the home country. (a) Calculate the investment per job created. (b) Evaluate the benefits of this investment for the host country.
items.answer: (a) US$133 333 (b) Jobs, wages, exports and skills are significant; but most profit leaves, linkages may be limited, and the factory may relocate if costs rise; benefits depend on upgrading and local supplier development.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that host countries gain more than home countries from the activities of TNCs. In your answer you may refer to jobs and FDI.
items.answer: For: Host countries gain jobs, FDI, technology and export growth (China, Vietnam, Ireland); industrialisation reduces poverty. Against: Home countries gain profits, cheaper goods and high-value jobs; host countries face low wages, repatriated profits, environmental damage and dependence. Conclusion: Both gain, but unequally; the balance depends on host country policy and the type of investment.

items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: A TNC invested US$200 million in an electronics factory in Mexico. It employs 6 000 local workers at an average of US$9 000 a year. 40% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$34 million, of which 66% is repatriated to the home country. Calculate the profit repatriated and the profit retained in the host country each year.
items.answer: repatriated US$22.4 million; retained US$11.6 million

items.stem: A TNC invested US$1000 million in an electronics factory in Morocco. It employs 1 500 local workers at an average of US$2 400 a year. 51% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$124 million, of which 89% is repatriated to the home country. Calculate the profit repatriated and the profit retained in the host country each year.
items.answer: repatriated US$110.4 million; retained US$13.6 million

items.stem: A TNC invested US$200 million in an electronics factory in Morocco. It employs 6 000 local workers at an average of US$2 400 a year. 28% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$30 million, of which 71% is repatriated to the home country. (a) Calculate the annual wage bill paid to local workers. (b) Calculate the profit repatriated and the profit retained in the host country each year.
items.answer: (a) US$14.4 million (b) repatriated US$21.3 million; retained US$8.7 million

items.stem: A TNC invested US$2500 million in an electronics factory in Vietnam. It employs 800 local workers at an average of US$2 400 a year. 32% of components are bought from local suppliers. Annual profit is US$205 million, of which 69% is repatriated to the home country. (a) Calculate the annual wage bill paid to local workers. (b) Calculate the investment per job created. (c) Explain why the share of components bought locally matters for the host country.
items.answer: (a) US$1.9 million (b) US$3 125 000 (c) Local purchases create linkages and multiplier effects, supporting local firms and jobs, and transferring technology and standards; low local content means an enclave with little wider benefit.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “moving business activities to another country”.
items.answer: Offshoring
items.markingKey: Offshoring: moving business activities to another country. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the reasons for the growth of TNCs. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “TNCs can shift profits to low-tax countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Falling transport and communication costs; trade liberalisation; access to markets and cheap labour and resources; economies of scale; mergers and acquisitions; government incentives. (b) Correct. Transfer pricing and subsidiaries in tax havens reduce tax paid.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “The NIDL means all stages of production stay in one country.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the reasons for the growth of TNCs.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. It is the spatial division of stages across countries. (b) Falling transport and communication costs; trade liberalisation; access to markets and cheap labour and resources; economies of scale; mergers and acquisitions; government incentives.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [4]

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $37, Mexico $7, China $10, Vietnam $4, Bangladesh $2. Assembling a pair of trainers takes 1.6 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 500 000 units a year. Calculate the labour cost per unit in each country.
items.answer: the USA: $59.2; Mexico: $11.2; China: $16; Vietnam: $6.4; Bangladesh: $3.2
items.markingKey: hourly cost × hours [2]

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $44, Mexico $4, China $10, Vietnam $3, Bangladesh $1.5. Assembling a pair of trainers takes 1 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 2 000 000 units a year. Calculate the annual saving in labour costs from assembling in the cheapest country rather than the USA.
items.answer: US$85 000 000 (Bangladesh)
items.markingKey: (US cost − cheapest cost) × 2 000 000 [2]

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $44, Mexico $7, China $8, Vietnam $4, Bangladesh $1.5. Assembling a pair of trainers takes 1.1 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 100 000 units a year. (a) Calculate the labour cost per unit in each country. (b) Explain how this example illustrates the new international division of labour.
items.answer: (a) the USA: $48.4; Mexico: $7.7; China: $8.8; Vietnam: $4.4; Bangladesh: $1.65 (b) Labour-intensive assembly is located in low-wage countries, while design, marketing and headquarters remain in HICs where skilled labour and markets are.
items.markingKey: (a) hourly cost × hours [2] (b) [3]

items.stem: Table 27.1 shows hourly labour costs (US$, including benefits) in manufacturing: the USA $35, Mexico $5, China $6, Vietnam $3, Bangladesh $2. Assembling a smartphone takes 1.6 hours of labour. A TNC plans to make 500 000 units a year. (a) Calculate the labour cost per unit in each country. (b) Calculate the annual saving in labour costs from assembling in the cheapest country rather than the USA.
items.answer: (a) the USA: $56; Mexico: $8; China: $9.6; Vietnam: $4.8; Bangladesh: $3.2 (b) US$26 400 000 (Bangladesh)
items.markingKey: (a) hourly cost × hours [2] (b) (US cost − cheapest cost) × 500 000 [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that TNCs are now more powerful than national governments.
items.answer: For: Largest TNC revenues exceed many countries’ GDPs; footloose investment gives bargaining power; tax avoidance; lobbying. Against: Governments control regulation, taxation, trade policy and market access (China’s controls, EU fines on tech firms, global minimum tax agreement 2021); TNCs depend on states for infrastructure and stability. Conclusion: TNCs have great influence, especially over small countries, but large states retain significant power.
items.markingKey: Marked out of 20 [20] using levels of response. Level 4 (16-20): detailed, accurate and well-integrated knowledge; well-chosen, place-specific examples; sustained evaluation and a strong, supported conclusion. Level 3 (11-15): clear knowledge with appropriate examples; evaluation present but uneven or not fully supported. Level 2 (6-10): some knowledge, mainly descriptive; limited or general examples; little evaluation. Level 1 (1-5): basic, fragmented points; no examples. Level 0: no creditable response. Indicative content: Largest TNC revenues exceed many countries’ GDPs; footloose investment gives bargaining power; tax avoidance; lobbying. Governments control regulation, taxation, trade policy and market access (China’s controls, EU fines on tech firms, global minimum tax agreement 2021); TNCs depend on states for infrastructure and stability. Judgement: TNCs have great influence, especially over small countries, but large states retain significant power.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “outsourcing services such as call centres, payroll, data processing and IT support, often to India or the Philippines”.
items.answer: Business process outsourcing (BPO)
items.markingKey: Business process outsourcing (BPO): outsourcing services such as call centres, payroll, data processing and IT support, often to India or the Philippines. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Outsourcing only involves manufacturing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Services such as call centres and software are widely outsourced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the risks of long global supply chains. (b) Explain why services are increasingly outsourced to countries such as India and the Philippines.
items.answer: (a) Disruption from pandemics, natural disasters, conflict, trade disputes and shipping blockages (Suez 2021); quality control and ethical problems; transport emissions. (b) Lower wages; large English-speaking, educated workforces; time-zone differences allowing 24-hour service; fast internet; government support for IT parks.

items.stem: Fig. 27.2 shows the share of the retail price (US$400) of a smartphone captured at each stage of its global production network: brand owner (design, software, marketing) 43%, component makers (chips, screen, memory) 30%, retail and distribution 13%, final assembly 3%, other costs 11%. (a) Calculate how many times more value the brand owner captures than final assembly. (b) Suggest why the brand owner keeps design and marketing in its home country.
items.answer: (a) 14.3 times (b) Highly skilled staff, universities and research clusters; protection of intellectual property; close to main markets and headquarters.

items.stem: “LICs gain little from participating in global production networks.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to value capture, upgrading and jobs.
items.answer: For: They capture a small share of value through low-wage assembly; footloose investment; poor working conditions (Rana Plaza 2013). Against: Jobs, export earnings, skills and technology transfer; upgrading (South Korea, Taiwan, China moved into higher value activities); India’s IT services sector. Conclusion: Gains are initially small, but countries that invest in skills and upgrading can capture more value over time.

Indicative content: They capture a small share of value through low-wage assembly; footloose investment; poor working conditions (Rana Plaza 2013). Jobs, export earnings, skills and technology transfer; upgrading (South Korea, Taiwan, China moved into higher value activities); India’s IT services sector. Judgement: Gains are initially small, but countries that invest in skills and upgrading can capture more value over time.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “home country”?
options: The country where a TNC has its headquarters.
The transfer of profits made in a host country back to the TNC’s home country.
Competition between countries to attract investment by lowering wages, taxes and environmental standards.
The spread of knowledge, skills and technology from foreign firms to local firms and workers.
items.answer: The country where a TNC has its headquarters.
items.markingKey: Home country: the country where a TNC has its headquarters. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the disadvantages of TNC investment for host countries. (b) Explain the impacts of globalisation on TNC home countries.
items.answer: (a) Low wages and poor conditions; profits repatriated; few local linkages; environmental damage; footloose plants may leave; competition harms local firms; political influence. (b) Profits and dividends flow home; cheaper imports for consumers; high-skilled HQ and R&D jobs; but deindustrialisation and job losses in manufacturing regions, rising inequality.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Globalisation benefits all groups in home countries equally.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the impacts of globalisation on TNC home countries.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Manufacturing workers may lose jobs while shareholders and consumers gain. (b) Profits and dividends flow home; cheaper imports for consumers; high-skilled HQ and R&D jobs; but deindustrialisation and job losses in manufacturing regions, rising inequality.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [3]
